---
title: Getting Started
---

## Installation

pycmdcheck needs Python 3.11 or later.

### Using pip

```bash
pip install pycmdcheck
```

### Using uv

Add pycmdcheck as a development dependency. A checker is not something your
package needs at run time.

```bash
uv add --dev pycmdcheck
```

To run it once without installing it, use `uvx`.

```bash
uvx pycmdcheck --profile triage path/to/package
```

## Your First Check

Start with the `triage` profile. It runs the 12 checks that only read files,
so it needs nothing installed besides pycmdcheck itself, and it executes no
code from the project.

```bash
pycmdcheck --profile triage
```

This is the output for a small package with a README, a license, a changelog,
two modules and one test file. The path on the first line is shortened here.

```
Checking package: .../riverplot (profile: triage)

┏━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃     ┃ Check           ┃ Message                                     ┃
┡━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│  ✓  │ changelog       │ Changelog present                           │
│  ℹ  │ ci              │ No CI configuration found                   │

└─────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

All checks passed!
Run again with --verbose to see a suggestion for each finding.
```

Add `--verbose`, or `-v` for short, to see the detail lines of each check.
They say what the check looked for and what it found. The option also prints
a suggestion for each finding, which is one sentence that says what to do
about it. This is what it adds for the `py_typed` note.

```
py_typed details:
  Package directory: src/riverplot
  Scanned 2 of 2 files: 2 of 2 public functions are annotated
  Suggestion: Add an empty file named py.typed to src/riverplot.
```

In the same output the `docs` note says that the package has no documentation
beyond its README. The `test_suite` check found the `tests/` directory. It
does not run the tests.

### A Full Run

```bash
pycmdcheck
```

With no profile, pycmdcheck runs every enabled check. That is all 20 built-in
checks. Eight of them do more than read files. They run your tests and
doctests, build the package, start a linter, a type checker and a formatter,
compare your imports with your declared dependencies, for which they read the
metadata of the installed packages, and request your project URLs over the
network.

Run a full run from the project's own environment, with the package and the
tools below installed. A check whose tool is missing is reported as skipped,
not as failed.

The `linting`, `typing` and `formatting` checks run the tool your project has
configured. They find it from files such as `pyproject.toml`, `ruff.toml` and
`mypy.ini`. A project that has configured no tool for one of them gets a
skipped result for that check and no list of findings from a tool it never
chose. To run a tool anyway, name it in `pyproject.toml`, as
[Configuration](configuration.qmd#tool-auto) shows.

### The Core Profile

```bash
pycmdcheck --profile core
```

The `core` profile runs 13 of the 20 checks. It leaves out `changelog`, `ci`,
`citation`, `community`, `doctests`, `python_versions` and `urls`. Like a full
run it executes code from the project, so it needs the same tools. Version
0.1.1 called this profile `default`. That name still works and prints a
warning.

This is the report for the small package from above. The package has
configured no linter, type checker or formatter. The run was also made from
an environment where neither the package nor the `build` module was
installed, which is the mistake the advice above is about.

```
┏━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃     ┃ Check        ┃ Message                                   ┃
┡━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│  ○  │ build        │ 'build' module not installed              │
│  ✓  │ dependencies │ No dependencies declared                  │
│  ✓  │ docs         │ Documentation present                     │
│  ○  │ formatting   │ No formatter configured                   │
│  ✓  │ license      │ License file present                      │
│  ○  │ linting      │ No linter configured                      │
│  ✓  │ metadata     │ Package metadata is valid                 │
│  ℹ  │ py_typed     │ Missing py.typed marker for typed package │
│  ✓  │ structure    │ Valid src layout structure                │
│  ✓  │ test_suite   │ Test suite present                        │
│  ✗  │ tests        │ Tests could not be collected              │
│  ○  │ typing       │ No type checker configured                │
│  ✓  │ version      │ Version 0.3.0 is consistent               │
└─────┴──────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

7 ok | 1 note | 1 error | 4 skipped

Failed: 1 error.
Run again with --verbose to see a suggestion for each finding.
```

Four checks are skipped. One lacks its tool and three have no tool
configured, and none of them counts against the package. A skipped check did
not look at anything, and its result says why. The one error comes from the
environment and not from the package. The tests import the package, the
package is not installed there, and so pytest could not collect them.

Two rows are about the tests. `test_suite` only looks for them, and `tests`
runs them. The `docs` check passes here because the `core` profile does not
turn on the look for documentation beyond the README, which `triage` does.

## Tools the Checks Need

| Check | Tool | Where pycmdcheck looks for it |
|-------|------|-------------------------------|
| `tests` | pytest, or Python's `unittest` when `runner = "unittest"` | `PATH` |
| `doctests` | pytest | `PATH` |
| `linting` | ruff, flake8 or pylint, whichever the project has configured | `PATH`. For ruff, also next to pycmdcheck's own Python. |
| `typing` | mypy or pyright, whichever the project has configured | `PATH` |
| `formatting` | ruff or black, whichever the project has configured | `PATH`, then next to pycmdcheck's own Python |
| `build` | the `build` module | The environment that runs pycmdcheck |

pytest, mypy, pyright, flake8 and pylint have to run where the project and its
dependencies are installed. That is why pycmdcheck takes them only from
`PATH`, the list of directories your shell searches for commands. Activate the
project's environment before you run pycmdcheck, or run it through a tool
that does so.

The other 14 checks need no tool. [Configuration](configuration.qmd#tool-auto)
explains how each check finds the project's tool and how to name one
yourself.

### Optional Dependencies

Four of the tools can be installed together with pycmdcheck, through its
extras.

```bash
pip install "pycmdcheck[linting]"         # ruff
pip install "pycmdcheck[typing-mypy]"     # mypy
pip install "pycmdcheck[typing-pyright]"  # pyright
pip install "pycmdcheck[build]"           # the build module
pip install "pycmdcheck[all]"             # all four
```

When ruff or the `build` module is missing, the skipped result names the
extra in a detail line. mypy and pyright have to run where your project and
its dependencies are installed, so their extras help only when pycmdcheck is
installed in that same environment.

There is no extra for pytest, flake8, pylint or black. pytest, flake8 and
pylint have to run in the project's environment, as said above, so install
the ones your project uses there.

Version 0.1.1 also had the extras `dev` and `docs`. They held the tools for
working on pycmdcheck itself and are dependency groups now. In a checkout of
the repository, `uv sync` installs the `dev` group.

## Using Python

```python
from pycmdcheck import check

report = check("riverplot", profile="triage")

print(f"Passed: {report.passed}")
print(f"Results: {len(report.results)} checks run")

for result in report.results:
    print(f"{result.status.symbol} {result.name}: {result.message}")
```

```
Passed: True
Results: 12 checks run
✓ changelog: Changelog present
ℹ ci: No CI configuration found
ℹ citation: No citation file found
ℹ community: 2 community file(s) not found in repository
ℹ docs: Some documentation improvements suggested
✓ license: License file present
✓ metadata: Package metadata is valid
ℹ py_typed: Missing py.typed marker for typed package
✓ python_versions: Python version requirement is current
✓ structure: Valid src layout structure
✓ test_suite: Test suite present
✓ version: Version 0.3.0 is consistent
```

`check()` takes the same choices as `--check` (`-c` for short), `--skip` (`-s`
for short) and `--profile` on the command line. `checks` and `skip` name
checks, and `profile` names a profile. Without any of them it performs a full
run. `report.passed` is `True` when no check returned an error. The package
offers no Python function that reads a `--config` file.

In Python each name is an item of its own in a list, as in
`checks=["metadata", "license"]`. A string with commas, such as
`"metadata,license"`, is not split as it is on the
[command line](cli.qmd#selecting-checks) and counts as one name.

A name in `checks` that no installed check has raises `ValueError`, and so
does an unknown profile name. This call misspells `license`.

```python
from pycmdcheck import check

try:
    check("riverplot", checks=["metadata", "licence"])
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)
```

```
Unknown check(s): licence. Available checks: build, changelog, ci, citation, community, dependencies, docs, doctests, formatting, imports, license, linting, metadata, py_typed, python_versions, structure, test_suite, tests, typing, urls, version
```

An unknown name in `skip` is different. It is logged as a warning and
ignored, so skipping a custom check that is not installed keeps working. The
command line is stricter. There an unknown name after `--skip` is a usage
error with exit code 2.

Each result also says what it found in a form a program can compare. Its
`findings` each carry a rule code, and a skipped result has a `skip_reason`.

```python
from pycmdcheck import check

report = check("riverplot", profile="triage")

for result in report.results:
    for finding in result.findings:
        print(f"{finding.status}: {finding.code}")
```

```
note: ci.missing
note: citation.missing
note: community.missing-contributing
note: community.missing-code-of-conduct
note: docs.missing-site
note: py_typed.missing
```

[Rule Codes](rules.qmd) lists every code and every skip reason.

## Understanding Check Results

Each check returns one of five statuses.

| Status | Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| OK | ✓ | The check found what it looked for |
| NOTE | ℹ | Something you can improve. Not a defect in itself. |
| WARNING | ⚠ | A likely problem that should be looked at |
| ERROR | ✗ | The check failed |
| SKIPPED | ○ | The check did not look at anything, for example because its tool is not installed or the project has not configured one |

By default only an error makes the command exit with a failure code.
[`--fail-on`](cli.qmd#fail-on) changes that. With `--fail-on warning`, for
example, a warning fails the run as well.

## Built-in Checks

`pycmdcheck --list` prints the checks that are installed. These are the 20
built-in ones and `imports`, a deprecated name that was merged into
`dependencies` and is left out of every run unless you ask for it by name.

```
                        Available Checks
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Name            ┃ Description                                 ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ build           │ Verify package builds successfully          │
│ changelog       │ Check for changelog or news file            │
│ ci              │ Check for CI configuration                  │
│ citation        │ Check for citation file                     │
│ community       │ Check for community health files            │
│ dependencies    │ Audit declared vs. actual dependencies      │
│ docs            │ Check documentation (README, docstrings)    │
│ doctests        │ Run doctests in package modules             │
│ formatting      │ Check code formatting (ruff format/black)   │
│ imports         │ Deprecated, use the dependencies check      │
│ license         │ Check for license file                      │
│ linting         │ Run code linting (ruff/flake8/pylint)       │
│ metadata        │ Validate package metadata (pyproject.toml)  │
│ py_typed        │ Check for PEP 561 py.typed marker           │
│ python_versions │ Check Python version support (EOL versions) │
│ structure       │ Validate package directory structure        │
│ test_suite      │ Check that the project has a test suite     │
│ tests           │ Run package tests (pytest/unittest)         │
│ typing          │ Run type checking (mypy/pyright)            │
│ urls            │ Validate project URLs are reachable         │
│ version         │ Verify version consistency                  │
└─────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

[Configuration](configuration.qmd) describes each check and its options, and
the [Command-Line Reference](cli.qmd#profiles) lists the profiles that select
subsets of them. To check repositories you do not own, a profile on the
command line is usually enough, and [`--config`](cli.qmd#config-file) takes
the settings from a file of your own when it is not.
